question.text: The end <math><mi>A</mi></math> of a rod <math><mi>A</mi><mi>B</mi></math> of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> is maintained at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>100</mn><mo> </mo><mo>°</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math> and the end <math><mi>B</mi><mi> </mi></math>at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>10</mn><mo> </mo><mo>°</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math>. What is the temperature (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>°</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math>) at a distance of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>60</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi></math> from the end <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>B</mi></math>?

solution.text:
The situation is given in the figure. Let θ be the temperature at point C.



We know that the rate flow of heat

Qt=KA(θ1-θ2)d

Here, K = coefficient of thermal conductivity

          A = area of cross-section

⇒   KA(100-θ)40=KA(θ-10)60

              100-θ2=θ-103

         300-3θ=2θ-20

                  5θ=320

                  θ=3205

                  θ=64℃
